planting.note: Pot into a well-drained mix and place in bright, indirect light; Decora is the classic broad-leaved rubber tree cultivar that has anchored the houseplant trade for decades and tolerates average indoor conditions better than newer colored-leaf sports.

directions: Site in bright, indirect light and let the top couple inches of potting mix dry between waterings, since soggy roots quickly cause leaf drop. Decora produces the wide, glossy, deep-green oval leaves with a prominent pale midrib that define the classic rubber plant look, growing as a single upright cane or multi-stem specimen that can reach ceiling height indoors over many years. It is more vigorous and forgiving of lower light than variegated or colored sports, making it a reliable large-scale foliage accent for shaded rooms or covered porches. Wipe the broad leaves periodically to keep pores open, and prune or air-layer tall canes to manage height and encourage branching.

common_name: Melany Rubber Plant (Compact Dwarf Rubber Tree)

planting.note: Grow in bright, indirect light in a well-drained container mix; Melany is a compact, densely-branching rubber tree sport well suited to tabletop or smaller-room use where full-size elastica cultivars would outgrow the space.

directions: Provide bright, indirect light and allow the potting mix to dry slightly between waterings, as Melany's tighter growth habit and smaller root mass make it easier to overwater than standard rubber trees. This dwarf, multi-branching sport carries narrower, dark green leaves with a slight downward curl and naturally produces side shoots without pinching, giving a fuller, bushier silhouette than the single-caned species. Its compact size makes it a good choice for desks, shelves, or shaded interior corners where a full-size rubber tree would be unwieldy. Rotate occasionally for even growth and wipe leaves to remove dust and keep them glossy.

planting.note: Grow as an interior tree or patio specimen in bright, indirect light; Danielle is a solid dark-green weeping fig cultivar selected for holding its leaves better through the low-light and relocation stress that typically triggers heavy leaf drop in this species.

directions: Place in the brightest indirect light available and keep watering and location consistent, since weeping figs are notorious for dropping leaves after any sudden change in light, temperature, or drafts. Danielle carries small, pointed, glossy dark-green leaves on gracefully arching, weeping branches and is prized among benjamina selections for being comparatively more stable once acclimated indoors. Let the top inch of soil dry before watering and avoid cold drafts or heating vents, both of which stress the foliage. Prune to shape and control size any time of year, as this cultivar responds well to pinching and tolerates being trained into standard or braided-trunk forms.

planting.note: Pot into a small container with well-drained mix and bright, indirect light; Too Little is a naturally dwarf weeping fig cultivar prized for bonsai and tabletop use, staying compact without the size and pruning demands of standard benjamina.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light and water when the top inch of mix dries out, keeping the small root system from either drying completely or sitting wet. Too Little produces tiny, densely packed dark-green leaves on slender, weeping twigs, giving it a naturally miniature, tree-like proportion that makes it a favorite subject for indoor bonsai and dish gardens without any special dwarfing technique required. It tolerates the light pruning and wiring typical of bonsai training and backbuds readily after cutting. Protect from cold drafts and sudden light changes, which can still cause leaf drop despite its compact habit.

common_name: Golden King Weeping Fig (Cream-Margined Variegated Ficus)

planting.note: Site in bright, indirect light to preserve variegation; Golden King is a weeping fig cultivar with broad creamy-yellow leaf margins that need brighter light than solid-green benjamina cultivars to avoid reverting to green.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light, since insufficient light causes the wide creamy-yellow leaf margins to fade and revert toward plain green. Golden King bears gently curled, glossy leaves broadly edged in ivory to pale yellow around a green center, giving a brighter, more luminous effect than the species on its gracefully weeping branches. Keep watering consistent, letting the top inch of mix dry between waterings, and avoid moving the plant or exposing it to cold drafts once it is settled, as sudden changes trigger leaf drop common to the species. Prune off any branches that revert to solid green to keep the variegation strong, and feed lightly during the growing season to support its color.
